title: What Keeps the Fire? Here Are Two Skillsets that Motivated Career Educators Have in Common
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Written in the thick of the pandemic's first stressful winter, this piece asks why some veteran teachers sustain enthusiasm for the work across decades while others burn out. Dave Stuart Jr. rejects the idea that longevity-with-joy is a matter of innate temperament or easier circumstances, arguing instead that it comes down to two learnable skillsets: depressurization (intelligent, practiced self-care) and workload modification (the willingness to question education's default, unsustainable workload assumptions). He's careful to separate the two; someone skilled only at depressurizing isn't necessarily a good teacher, since contemporary teaching's default workload will produce 80-plus-hour weeks if followed uncritically. The teachers who last, in his account, are those who've built real expertise in focusing, streamlining, satisficing, and skipping non-essential work, turning former stressors into manageable 'pieces of the puzzle.' Stuart frames both skills as trainable rather than fixed, setting up a course he was developing on the subject.
points: Stuart's central thesis is that career-long teacher motivation comes down to two learnable skillsets, depressurization (intelligent self-care) and workload modification (questioning default workload assumptions), not innate temperament or easier circumstances.

He explicitly separates the two skills: being good at depressurizing doesn't make someone a good teacher unless it's paired with workload modification, since default teaching workload is structurally unsustainable at 80+ hours a week.

Teachers who sustain the 'fire' across decades are reframed not as exceptions with rare genetic dispositions but as practitioners who've built expertise in questioning 'popular assumptions of education.'

Stuart is skeptical of generic 'self-care' content, distinguishing between people who deploy isolated tips and tricks and those who've internalized depressurization as an intelligent, experimental practice.
quotes: Externally, teaching affords us the unmatched privilege of contributing to the education of human beings. Few endeavors are as wrought with possibility as the teaching of people.
Internally, teaching is so difficult — emotionally, socially, intellectually, spiritually, physically — that it affords us rich soil within which to cultivate the inner life.
What happened was difficulty that we hadn't bargained for. We knew it would be hard — but 2020 hard? Poor administrator hard? Initiative fatigue hard? Cameras off hard? Endless paperwork hard?

The difference is skilled and thoughtful inner work, in two particular areas: depressurization and workload modification. Folks who are good at these two things tend to love and be good at their jobs and their lives.
But if you're only good at depressurization, you're not necessarily going to be a good teacher. Being good at your job and a generally depressurized person takes another skill: workload modification.

If you do everything you're "supposed" to do, just as you're "supposed" to do it, they know you'll work eighty-plus hours per week and you won't last very long. These people aren't playing a short game, though. This is their life's work.

And as they learn, their abilities improve: they can focus better, streamline better, satisfice better, skip better. Things that used to cost them lost sleep become simply parts of the job, pieces of the puzzle they're still working out.
